item.title: Apple frees Siri from domains: arbitrary app intents and Markdown skills are coming
item.description:
Apple is finally freeing Siri from its domain system. Before iOS 27.3, an app could only expose Siri actions that fit into one of Apple's blessed domains — a model that never worked for apps that don't fit into neat boxes. Now developers can supply arbitrary app intent definitions to the system, and even provide Markdown skill files to help Siri know how and when to use them.

The practical difference is striking. In Jordan Morgan's Elite Hoops app, a coach used to have to say "add a player to a team" and then answer Siri's follow-up questions for each detail, or wire steps together in a shortcut. Now a single request — "add Maya to the Tigers, she's a point guard, number 12, then open that team" — can be handled conversationally, with Siri finding the team, filling in the details, and chaining the actions itself. Follow-ups work too: "find my press break plays" and then "email Coach Jones those notes" carry context across turns without repeating the app name.

The other half of the story is App Skills: a SKILL.md file bundled with the app that tells Siri how to use its actions together — what a coach means, when to ask a follow-up, which actions to combine. Developers add a Skills Bundle to the app target in Xcode, and Siri reads the description to decide when the skill applies, then follows the instructions. The app intents still do the work; the skill is guidance on top. For developers who have waited years for Siri to handle real apps, this is the direction that finally makes sense.

Sources

  • Swiftjective-C: Finally, Apple Frees us from Domains

item.title: Agent hooks are the reliable way to make AI coding tools follow your rules
item.description:
SwiftLee's Antoine van der Lee explains agent hooks: small scripts your AI coding tool runs automatically when something happens — before a shell command executes, when the agent finishes a task, and so on. Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex all support them, and they work the same way across tools.

The key insight is reliability. Telling an agent a rule in a prompt or a CLAUDE.md file works only when the agent remembers to follow it; a hook enforces it every time, deterministically. If you want every commit message formatted a certain way, every file checked before it lands, or a reminder injected at exactly the right moment, hooks — not hopes — are how you get it.

Sources

  • SwiftLee: Agent hooks in Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex explained

item.title: Beyond basic unwrapping: interesting ways to use Swift optionals
item.description:
Swift by Sundell has a new showcase of interesting ways to use optionals that go beyond simply unwrapping values. Rather than rehashing the basics, the piece explores more creative and expressive uses of the language's optional-handling tools.

For Swift developers, it's a chance to rethink a feature used in nearly every codebase — and pick up patterns that can make optional-heavy code cleaner and more intentional. If optionals feel like boilerplate in your code, this is a concise read worth working through.

Sources

  • Swift by Sundell: Interesting ways of using Swift optionals
